lesson.title: Knowing When to Stop: The Sentinel Value Pattern
lesson.summary: The sentinel value pattern uses a special input, one that would never appear as real data, to signal a loop that it is time to stop.
lesson.body:
Some loops know exactly how many times to run before they start, like looping over a list of five items five times. Other loops have no such guarantee. A program that keeps asking the user for numbers to add together, or keeps reading lines from a file until there are no more, cannot know in advance how many iterations it needs. The sentinel value pattern solves this by picking a special value, one that will never show up as legitimate data, and using its appearance as the signal to stop looping.

This pattern depends directly on the while loop, because a while loop's condition is checked fresh before every iteration rather than being fixed by the size of a sequence in advance. The classic structure is while True combined with a break statement: the loop starts as an infinite loop, and the only way out is an explicit break triggered when the sentinel is detected. This might look strange at first (why write a loop that never stops on its own?) but it is exactly the right shape when the stopping condition can only be evaluated after you have already read the next piece of input.

Here is a program that adds numbers typed in by a user until they type the word 'done', which acts as the sentinel because it is not a number the program would otherwise expect to sum:

total = 0
while True:
    entry = input("Enter a number (or 'done' to finish): ")
    if entry == "done":
        break
    total += int(entry)
print("Sum:", total)

Suppose the user types 5, then 10, then done. On the first pass entry is "5", it does not match the sentinel, so total becomes 0 + 5, which is 5. On the second pass entry is "10", again not the sentinel, so total becomes 5 + 10, which is 15. On the third pass entry is "done", the condition entry == "done" is True, and break exits the loop immediately, skipping the addition entirely. The program prints Sum: 15.

Choosing a good sentinel matters. It has to be a value that could never legitimately occur in the real data the loop is processing, or the loop will stop too early and silently drop valid input. A grade-averaging program that used 0 as a sentinel would break the moment a student actually scored a zero. That is why programs reading numbers often use a string sentinel like 'done' or 'quit', or a clearly impossible number like -1 when zero and positive numbers are both valid, since -1 cannot be confused with a real grade or count.

The sentinel value pattern connects back to the counter pattern and other loop patterns in a practical way: once you can stop a loop based on the data itself rather than a fixed number of repetitions, you can combine that same while True and break structure with a counter to also report how many real entries were processed before the sentinel appeared, which is a common next step once this basic pattern feels comfortable.
